title: Transport in GCAM, in full
summary: Passenger and freight transport in GCAM 9.1 in full: the nesting tree, the cost per passenger-km, the value of time, two kinds of logit, and how much travel is demanded.
outcomes: Draw GCAM's passenger transport nesting tree from service to technology
Build a technology's cost per passenger-km from non-fuel cost, fuel and load factor
Add the value of time to get a mode's generalised cost, using GCAM's 2,000-hour wage rule
Explain where relative-cost and absolute-cost logits are used, and how service demand responds to income and price
narration_en: Transport in GCAM is a tree. At the top is passenger service, measured in passenger-kilometres, and freight service, in tonne-kilometres. Passenger service is shared among walking, cycling, rail, domestic aviation and road; road splits into buses and light vehicles; light vehicles split into two and three wheelers and four wheelers; and at the bottom, technologies such as petrol, hybrid, battery electric and fuel-cell cars compete. Each technology's cost per passenger-kilometre is its non-fuel cost plus its fuel cost, divided by how many people ride in the vehicle. Then GCAM adds the cost of time: an hourly wage, which is income per person divided by two thousand hours, times a multiplier for each mode, divided by the mode's speed. As people get richer, time costs more, so fast modes gain. Modes compete through relative-cost logits, and technologies within a mode through absolute-cost logits. Finally, total travel grows with income and falls with price. In version 9.1 the effective vehicle costs and intensities come from a 2023 harmonisation file, not only from the original UC Davis data.
narration_ar: النقل في نموذج GCAM شجرة متفرّعة. في أعلاها خدمة نقل الركاب مقيسة بالراكب-كيلومتر، وخدمة نقل البضائع مقيسة بالطن-كيلومتر. وتتوزع خدمة الركاب بين المشي وركوب الدراجات والقطارات والطيران الداخلي والطرق؛ وتنقسم الطرق إلى حافلات ومركبات خفيفة؛ وتنقسم المركبات الخفيفة إلى مركبات ذات عجلتين أو ثلاث ومركبات ذات أربع عجلات؛ وفي الأسفل تتنافس التقنيات مثل السيارات العاملة بالبنزين والهجينة والكهربائية بالبطاريات وبخلايا الوقود. وتكلفة كل تقنية لكل راكب-كيلومتر هي تكلفتها غير الوقودية مضافًا إليها تكلفة الوقود، مقسومة على عدد الركاب في المركبة. ثم يضيف النموذج تكلفة الوقت: أجر الساعة، وهو دخل الفرد مقسومًا على ألفي ساعة، مضروبًا في معامل خاص بكل وسيلة، ومقسومًا على سرعة الوسيلة. وكلما زاد الثراء ارتفعت قيمة الوقت فتكسب الوسائل السريعة. وتتنافس الوسائل عبر نموذج لوجيت للتكلفة النسبية، وتتنافس التقنيات داخل الوسيلة الواحدة عبر لوجيت للتكلفة المطلقة. وأخيرًا ينمو إجمالي السفر مع الدخل وينخفض مع السعر. وفي الإصدار 9.1 تأتي التكاليف والكثافات الفعلية للمركبات من ملف مواءمة صدر عام 2023، وليس فقط من بيانات جامعة كاليفورنيا في ديفيس الأصلية.

diagram.title: GCAM's passenger transport tree, with freight beside it
diagram.caption: Each level shares its parent's service by a logit; time cost enters at the mode level.

nodes.label: Passenger service
nodes.detail: Total passenger-km demanded, driven by income (elasticity 1.0) and price (−1.25) in A54.demand.csv. Shared among modes by a relative-cost logit (exponent −2).

nodes.label: Walk and cycle
nodes.detail: No money cost, but slow: the time-value multiplier 1.066 times the wage, over 4.8 or 15 km/h.

nodes.label: Passenger rail
nodes.detail: Low money cost per pkm, multiplier 0.80, door-to-door speed around 42 km/h in the Middle East.

nodes.label: Domestic aviation
nodes.detail: High money cost, multiplier 1.244 (includes waiting), speed about 197 km/h door to door.

nodes.label: Road
nodes.detail: Buses and light vehicles share road passenger service (logit exponent −4).

nodes.label: Bus
nodes.detail: Liquids, natural gas and battery-electric buses compete inside the Bus mode.

nodes.label: Light vehicles
nodes.detail: trn_pass_road_LDV splits into two/three-wheelers and four-wheelers (exponent −4). Time value is added once, at the 4W node.

nodes.label: Car technologies
nodes.detail: Absolute-cost logit (exponent −8) on cost per pkm. BEV share-weight 0 until 2025, 1 from 2030; FCEV rises to 0.5 by 2050.

nodes.label: Freight
nodes.detail: Freight modes (road trucks by size, rail, domestic ship) compete on cost without a time term.

nodes.label: International
nodes.detail: International aviation and shipping draw on the same refined-liquids pool; there is no separate aviation fuel in the release.

tour.text: Start from passenger service: billion passenger-km, growing with income and falling with price.
Modes share the service by a relative-cost logit on generalised cost: money plus time.
Road splits into buses and light vehicles; light vehicles into two/three-wheelers and four-wheelers.
At the bottom, car technologies compete by an absolute-cost logit on cost per passenger-km.
Freight is a parallel tree measured in tonne-km, with no time term. International aviation and shipping use the general liquids pool.

sections.heading: The nesting tree
sections.html:
Each demand is met by a tree of supplysectors, tranSubsectors (modes or size classes) and tranTechnologies (drivetrains). At each branch point a logit shares the market among the branches by cost. Pass-through nodes ("road", "LDV", "4W") simply hand the choice down one level.

sections.heading: Step 1: the cost of a technology per passenger-km
sections.html:
Start with one vehicle. It burns I units of fuel per vehicle-km at fuel price Pf, costs N per vehicle-km to own and maintain, and carries L people on average (the load factor). The cost of one passenger-km is the cost of one vehicle-km shared among the passengers:

Pj = ( Pf · Ij + Nj ) ÷ Lj(3.3)

In the code this is TranTechnology (cvs/objects/technologies/source/tran_technology.cpp); in the XML, I is the coefficient of the fuel input, N the input-cost of the minicam-non-energy-input named "non-energy", and L the loadFactor. The non-fuel cost is built in gcamdata (zenergy_L154.transportation_UCD.R) from capital and operating costs: capital is annualised with a 10 % discount rate over 10 years and divided by the distance a vehicle travels each year.

N = [ (purchase + other + infrastructure) × CRF(10 %, 10 y) + maintenance + registration and insurance + tolls ] ÷ annual vkm(3.4)

Data: UCD_trn_data_CORE.csv (petrol car, operating costs, intensities, load factor 2.33, 14,000 vkm/yr) and OTAQ_trn_data_EMF37.csv (BEV purchase, other and charger costs), Middle East, Compact Car, 2020, v9.1. Fuel prices are illustrative round numbers, not GCAM outputs.

sections.heading: Step 2: the generalised cost of a mode
sections.html:
A traveller also pays with time. GCAM converts income into an hourly wage, W = GDP per person ÷ 2,000 hours (40 hours × 50 weeks, hard-coded in TranSubsector::getTimeValue), scales it by a time-value multiplier V and divides by the mode's door-to-door speed S:

Pi = Σj sji Pji + W · Vi ÷ Si,    W = GDP per capita ÷ (40 h × 50 wk)(3.5)

The time term is added only where addTimeValue = 1: on passenger modes and on the 4W node (once, at the LDV-versus-other-modes level), never on freight or on drivetrain choice. Since v8.5 the GDP used here is deflated from 1990 to 1975 dollars inside the code.

sections.heading: Step 3: sharing — two kinds of logit
sections.html:
At every branch, shares follow a logit. GCAM has two forms (documentation, Economic Choice). The relative-cost logit compares cost ratios; the absolute-cost logit compares cost differences, scaled by a base value p0:

relative: si = αi Piγ ÷ Σk αk Pkγ     absolute: si = αi eγ Pi/p0 ÷ Σk αk eγ Pk/p0(3.6)

Which form applies where? In the gcamdata files every tranSubsector (choice among drivetrains) is set to absolute-cost-logit, as is the trn_pass_road_LDV_4W sector. The other supplysectors leave logit.type empty, and gcamdata then fills in the default, the relative-cost logit (add_logit_tables_xml in R/xml.R). So mode choice is relative, drivetrain choice is absolute. The absolute form copes with costs that can be near zero or negative, which matters once carbon prices and subsidies enter.

sections.heading: Step 4: how much travel
sections.html:
The total service demand grows with income and population and falls with the aggregate price of the service (the average cost that the nest passes up). In minicam_price_elasticity_function.cpp:

Dt = Dt−1 · (Yt/Yt−1)α · (Pt/Pt−1)β · (Nt/Nt−1)(3.7)

Y is GDP per person, P the service price, N population (only for per-capita demands); α and β are the income and price elasticities in the table above. Because α = 1 for passenger travel, travel per person grows as fast as income unless prices rise.

callouts.title: Why this matters
callouts.html: For a Saudi driver in our worked example, owning and running a compact petrol car costs about $0.29 per passenger-km, of which fuel is only $0.014. The time spent driving, valued at a wage, costs almost as much as the car itself: $0.23 per passenger-km. In GCAM, cheap fuel barely moves the mode choice; speed and income do.

callouts.title: Pitfall
callouts.html: Biofuels, e-fuels and ammonia are not transport technologies. Low-carbon liquids reach vehicles only through the refining sector, which blends oil, gas- and coal-to-liquids, ethanols, biodiesel and FT biofuels into one pool, refined liquids enduse. Aviation and shipping draw on the same pool as cars, so a sustainable-aviation-fuel mandate needs a model change. Core v9.1 has no power-to-liquids or DAC-to-liquids technology, and ammonia is an industrial product, not a transport fuel.

callouts.title: Worked calculation
callouts.html:
Worked example: a compact car in the Middle East, 2020 (2005$)

  1. CRF = 0.10 × 1.110 ÷ (1.110 − 1) = 0.1627.
  2. Petrol car capital: 31,342 purchase + 10,970 other = 42,312 $; × 0.1627 = 6,886 $/yr.
  3. Operating: 448 maintenance + 1,550 registration and insurance = 1,998 $/yr.
  4. Non-fuel per vehicle-km: (6,886 + 1,998) ÷ 14,000 km = 0.635 $/vkm.
  5. Fuel: 3.32 MJ/vkm × 10 $/GJ (illustrative) = 0.0332 $/vkm.
  6. Per passenger-km: (0.635 + 0.0332) ÷ 2.33 persons = 0.286 $/pkm.
  7. Battery car, same steps (capital 51,991 $ incl. 1,409 $ charger; 1.03 MJ/vkm at 25 $/GJ): 0.328 $/pkm.

Answer: the BEV is 15 % dearer per pkm in 2020; capital is 74 % of the petrol car's cost and fuel only 5 %

callouts.title: Research note
callouts.html: Which file sets the cost you think you are changing? For cars, trucks, buses, rail, aviation and ships, gcamdata overwrites the UC Davis (UCD) values with OTAQ_trn_data_EMF37.csv: "MODIFIED intensity and capital cost … based on AUTONOMIE and TEMPO harmonization" (source workbook dated 14 March 2023). In our example the petrol car's costs still come from UCD (no OTAQ row), but the BEV's come from OTAQ. Edit the wrong file and nothing changes.

callouts.title: Worked calculation
callouts.html:
Worked example: the price of time

  1. GDP per person $20,000 (illustrative) ÷ 2,000 h = W = $10 per hour.
  2. Car: 10 × 0.82 ÷ 35 km/h = 0.234 $/pkm.
  3. Bus: 10 × 0.808 ÷ 21 km/h = 0.385 $/pkm — slower, so time costs more than the bus fare.
  4. Rail: 10 × 0.80 ÷ 42 km/h = 0.190 $/pkm.
  5. Double the income and every time cost doubles; fast modes gain on slow ones.

Answer: income growth pushes travellers towards faster modes even if money costs stay the same

callouts.title: Worked calculation
callouts.html:
Worked example: calibrating a share-weight

  1. Observed 2021: BEVs take 1 % of new car pkm, though they cost 15 % more (pBEV = 1.15 p0).
  2. With αICE = 1 and γ = −8: sBEV/sICE = αBEV · e−8(1.15 − 1) = αBEV · e−1.2.
  3. Set the ratio to 0.01/0.99 = 0.0101: αBEV = 0.0101 ÷ 0.3012 = 0.0335.
  4. Check: share = 0.010, the observed 1 %.
  5. Now the future path of αBEV (0.034 → 1 by 2030 in the s-curve) does as much work as any cost change.

Answer: αBEV ≈ 0.034; the share-weight hides everything costs do not explain

callouts.title: In GCAM
callouts.html:
Where it lives (v9.1). Chunks: input/gcamdata/R/zenergy_L154.transportation_UCD.R (calibration, costs, intensities by UCD region) and zenergy_L254.transportation_UCD.R (level-2 tables such as L254.StubTranTechCost, L254.StubTranTechLoadFactor, L254.tranSubsectorVOTT, L254.IncomeElasticity_trn); XML writer zenergy_xml_transportation_UCD_CORE.R → transportation_UCD_CORE.xml, _SSP1, _SSP3, _SSP5. Assumptions: A54.*_revised.csv (the _revised files are the ones used), UCD_trn_data_*.csv, OTAQ_trn_data_EMF37.csv, mappings UCD_techs_revised.csv, UCD_ctry.csv.

Calibration. IEA transport energy by country and fuel is split into UCD modes, size classes and technologies with 2005 UCD shares, scaled to GCAM end-use energy, converted to vkm (÷ intensity) and pkm (× load factor); share-weights then reproduce each base year to 2021. Parameters exist for 14 UCD regions and are mapped to GCAM's 32: Saudi values are generic "Middle East" values.

callouts.title: Pitfall
callouts.html: Two documentation pages disagree with the code. en_technologies.html still gives 1990$ and BTU per vehicle-km (v8.2 units). And the docs' general advice that passenger transport suits the relative-cost logit is true for mode choice but not for drivetrain choice, which the input files set to the absolute-cost form. Always check the XML you are running.

callouts.title: Try it
callouts.html:
1. Using Eq. 3.3, what happens to the petrol car's cost per pkm if the load factor falls from 2.33 to 2.0 (the 2050 value)? (Answer key.)
  2. With γ = −8, how much cheaper must a BEV be than a petrol car for it to take 80 % of the pair, with equal share-weights?
  3. Why does a carbon price of $200/tCO2 change car choice less than a 30 % change in battery-car capital cost? Use Figure 3.3.

takeaways: Passenger transport is a tree: service → modes → road → light vehicles → 4W → technologies
Technology cost per pkm = (non-fuel cost + fuel price × intensity) ÷ load factor
Mode cost adds wage × time-value multiplier ÷ speed, with wage = GDP per person ÷ 2,000 h
Modes compete by relative-cost logits; technologies inside a mode by absolute-cost logits
Edit OTAQ_trn_data_EMF37.csv, not only the UC Davis data, when changing most vehicle costs

quiz.q: GCAM's hourly wage for the value of time is…
quiz.explain: TranSubsector uses GDP per capita over 40 hours × 50 weeks.

quiz.q: Car occupancy (load factor) rises from 1.5 to 2.0. The cost per passenger-km…
quiz.explain: Cost per vkm is divided by people per vehicle: 1.5/2.0 = 0.75.

quiz.q: Which logit type is used for technologies inside the Car mode?
quiz.explain: A54.tranSubsector_logit_revised.csv sets absolute-cost logits within modes (Car −8).

quiz.q: Why do faster modes gain share as countries get richer, even with unchanged prices?
options: Time costs more as wages rise
quiz.explain: The time term grows with the wage, penalising slow modes.

quiz.q: Where do most vehicle costs and intensities in GCAM 9.1 come from?
quiz.explain: gcamdata overwrites UCD values with the 2023 EMF37/Autonomie/TEMPO harmonisation for most modes.

code.title: Generalised cost and mode shares, GCAM-style
code.source:
# Generalised cost of passenger modes, GCAM-style (illustrative numbers, 2005$)
# money cost per pkm + wage x time-value multiplier / speed;  wage = GDP per person / 2,000 h
gdp_per_person = 18000          # $ per year
wage = gdp_per_person / 2000    # $ per hour

#        name     money $/pkm  multiplier  speed km/h
modes = [("Walk",  0.000,      1.066,       4.8),
         ("Bus",   0.070,      0.808,      22.0),
         ("Rail",  0.015,      0.800,      42.0),
         ("Car",   0.294,      0.820,      35.0)]

costs = {}
for name, money, mult, speed in modes:
    time_cost = wage * mult / speed
    costs[name] = money + time_cost
    print(f"{name:5s} money {money:.3f} + time {time_cost:.3f} = {costs[name]:.3f} $/pkm")

# Relative-cost logit across modes (exponent -2, equal share-weights for illustration)
w = {k: c ** -2 for k, c in costs.items()}
total = sum(w.values())
print("shares:", {k: round(v / total, 3) for k, v in w.items()})

# Double income: time becomes dearer, so slow modes lose share
wage2 = 2 * wage
c2 = {n: m + wage2 * v / s for n, m, v, s in modes}
w2 = {k: c ** -2 for k, c in c2.items()}
print("shares at 2x income:", {k: round(v / sum(w2.values()), 3) for k, v in w2.items()})
code.explain: Money cost per pkm plus wage × time-value multiplier ÷ speed, then a relative-cost logit across modes. Share-weights are equal here, so rail's large share is an artefact: in GCAM, share-weights are calibrated to observed shares. Try doubling income.
